claims.text: Al0.1CrCoFeNi is predominantly chemically clustered before the intervention.
The clustered initial state is equivalent to a random chemical distribution.
High-strain compressive deformation can induce a clustering-to-ordering transition in Al0.1CrCoFeNi.
Compression-induced ordering in Al0.1CrCoFeNi involves increased unlike-pair correlations and decreased like-pair correlations.
Compression at 300–500 °C and high strain rates induces the clustering-to-ordering transition.
Annealing after high-strain compression preserves or promotes the compression-induced ordered state.
Under tensile loading, clustering remains dominant in Al0.1CrCoFeNi.
Simple or full annealing retains a more clustered, less ordered chemical distribution in Al0.1CrCoFeNi.
Increased local chemical ordering makes electron density more homogeneous within micro-regions.
Chemical ordering creates regions with modified local electron densities.
Modified local electron densities caused by ordering modulate the electron–phonon coupling constant.
The electron–phonon coupling constant governs Cooper-pair formation in this alloy.
Ordering-induced changes in electron–phonon coupling shift the superconducting transition temperature.
Ordering-induced changes in electron–phonon coupling alter the superconducting gap distribution.
Compression-treated samples will have a significantly different Tc than tensile-loaded and annealed controls.
Compression-treated samples will have a broadened or otherwise distinct superconducting gap distribution relative to tensile-loaded and annealed controls.
The superconducting effect is detectable only when processing induces the clustering-to-ordering transition.
Other strain-induced defects can obscure superconducting effects caused by chemical ordering.
A lack of statistically significant Tc or gap-distribution differences, or a lack of correlation with ordering, would falsify the hypothesis.
